newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: UK foreign minister set to miss parliamentary vote.
newsitem.headline: UK foreign minister set to miss parliamentary vote.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind will miss a parliamentary vote in London on Monday crucial to the beleaguered Conservative government unless he cuts short a planned visit to Hong Kong.
Rifkind, in Singapore for a meeting of Asian and European foreign ministers, told Reuters Television he would stay in the city-state until Saturday and then be in Hong Kong until Tuesday.
Britain's opposition Labour Party has called a parliamentary debate and vote for Monday evening over Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's handling of the "mad cow" crisis.
If Labour wins the debate, Hogg would be forced to resign and a vote of no-confidence in Prime Minister John Major's administration could be triggered later in the week.
Asked on Thursday if he would be back in Britain for the vote at the end of the debate on Monday, Rifkind said: "No.
"I am due to be in Hong Kong until Tuesday and then I will be returning to the United Kingdom."
British diplomats told Reuters that Rifkind's absence would not matter because Robin Cook, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, was also expected to miss the vote.
Cook had accepted an invitation to visit Singapore from Monday, they said.
But Singapore sources said Cook had cancelled his visit to Singapore at the request of Labour parliamentary officials anxious to win Monday's parliamentary vote.
Cook, a political adversary but long-time friend of Rifkind and fellow Scottish member of parliament, used to have a "pairing" arrangement with the foreign minister.
These arrangements were scrapped by Labour recently in an effort to put pressure on Major in the run-up to the British general election, which must be held by May 22.
If the government loses Monday night's vote, Major's position would be precarious.
Major is believed to favour May 1 for the election, just three weeks ahead of the deadline. The Conservatives have been in office for 18 years.

But, with Labour some 20 points up in opinion polls, there is speculation Major may call the election earlier to avoid an expected defeat in a parliamentary by-election scheduled in Wirral, northeast England, on February 27.
The Conservatives are tied with all the opposition parties in parliament, although they have 51 seats more than Labour.

But if Labour wins the backing of other opposition parties, many of whom are furious at the government's handling of the mad cow crisis, Major would have to ensure that all his members of parliament, even MPs who are seriously ill, turn up to vote.
